summary: Describes how to build PPP sessions and encapsulate PPP packets over Ethernet. It is widely used by broadband providers to connect customers over shared Ethernet-style links. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: PPPoE lets a host establish a PPP session through an Ethernet network. A discovery exchange finds an Access Concentrator and assigns the identifier used for the session traffic.

subtitle: A discovery handshake and session format for carrying PPP over Ethernet.

tldr.problem: Access providers wanted PPP sessions with per-user access control and billing over shared Ethernet connections.
tldr.mechanism: A Host discovers and selects an Access Concentrator, receives a session identifier, and then carries PPP frames in Ethernet frames for that session.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2516 describes PPPoE as an Informational specification and defines separate Discovery and PPP Session stages.

today: RFC 2516 is an Informational RFC published in February 1999. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Carry PPP over Ethernet
sections.content:
Providers may want several hosts at a site to share an Ethernet access device while keeping PPP’s per-user session interface, access control, and billing. PPPoE lets each host use its own PPP stack while connecting through a simple bridging device to a remote Access Concentrator.

PPP expects a point-to-point relationship, while Ethernet can connect multiple devices. PPPoE’s Discovery stage finds the remote peer’s Ethernet address and establishes a session identifier so the two endpoints can use Ethernet as a point-to-point PPP connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Several hosts can share Ethernet while each one establishes its own PPP session with the provider. The discovery exchange identifies the provider endpoint and the session.

sections.title: Discovery and PPP Session Stages
sections.content:
PPPoE has a Discovery stage followed by a PPP Session stage. During discovery, the Host finds one or more Access Concentrators, selects one, and establishes the SESSION_ID and peer Ethernet address. Discovery remains stateless until the PPP session is established.

Once the PPP session begins, both the Host and Access Concentrator allocate resources for a PPP virtual interface. PPP traffic then uses the session identifier selected during discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: First, a host finds and selects an Access Concentrator and gets a session identifier. Then the two sides use that identifier for PPP traffic.

sections.title: The PPPoE Header and Discovery Tags
sections.content:
Discovery Ethernet frames use EtherType 0x8863, while session frames use 0x8864. The PPPoE header contains version, type, code, SESSION_ID, and LENGTH fields. The session ID stays fixed for the session, and 0xffff is reserved.

Discovery payloads contain zero or more tags, each with a type, length, and value. A receiver must ignore an unknown tag unless the RFC says otherwise, which allows new tags to be added without changing the version.
sections.plainLanguage: The EtherType distinguishes discovery traffic from session traffic. A PPPoE header identifies the message and its session, while discovery tags carry extra labeled information.

sections.title: The Discovery Exchange and Session End
sections.content:
The Host broadcasts PADI to request a service. Each Access Concentrator that can serve it replies with a unicast PADO offer. The Host chooses one and sends PADR; the selected Access Concentrator returns PADS with a unique SESSION_ID. Either side can later send PADT to terminate the session.

After discovery, PPP frames use the session EtherType and the assigned ID. The PPP MTU must not exceed 1492 octets because the Ethernet payload also carries the PPPoE header and PPP Protocol ID. When LCP ends, the Host must return to Discovery to start another session.
sections.plainLanguage: The host asks for service, receives offers, chooses an Access Concentrator, and receives a session identifier. If the session ends, the host must run discovery again before starting another one.

sections.title: Protecting Access Concentrator Resources
sections.content:
An Access Concentrator may use an AC-Cookie tag to check that a Host address is reachable and to limit concurrent sessions from that address. The RFC leaves the cookie algorithm to implementations and notes that cookies cannot prevent every denial-of-service attack.

The concentrator may also avoid revealing which services it offers to unauthenticated Hosts. The RFC recommends accepting requests without refusing based on the Service-Name tag and echoing the requested value.
sections.plainLanguage: A concentrator can use a cookie to limit some unwanted session requests. The RFC notes that this measure does not prevent every denial-of-service attack.
